🔢 Binary ↔ Decimal Octet Cheat Sheet

Powers of 2 (one octet = 8 bits)

Every IPv4 octet is 8 bits. Write these 8 values above each bit position — they never change.

Bit #87654321
Value1286432168421

Binary → Decimal

Add up the column values wherever the bit is a 1. Skip the columns that are 0.

11000000
= 128 + 64
= 192
11001101
= 128 + 64 + 8 + 4 + 1
= 205

Decimal → Binary

Start from 128 and work down. If the number is ≥ the column value, write a 1 and subtract it; otherwise write a 0 and move to the next column.

205 ≥ 128 → 1, remainder 77
77 ≥ 64 → 1, remainder 13
13 < 32 → 0
13 < 16 → 0
13 ≥ 8 → 1, remainder 5
5 ≥ 4 → 1, remainder 1
1 < 2 → 0
1 ≥ 1 → 1, remainder 0
Result: 11001101 (check: 128+64+8+4+1 = 205 ✓)

Full CIDR ↔ subnet mask reference (/1 – /32)

The slash number is how many of the 32 total bits are 1s (network bits). E.g. /24 = the first 24 bits are 1s = the first three octets are 255, last octet is 0 → 255.255.255.0. Yes — your professor is right.

CIDR/1/2/3/4/5/6/7/8
Mask128.0.0.0192.0.0.0224.0.0.0240.0.0.0248.0.0.0252.0.0.0254.0.0.0255.0.0.0
CIDR/9/10/11/12/13/14/15/16
Mask255.128.0.0255.192.0.0255.224.0.0255.240.0.0255.248.0.0255.252.0.0255.254.0.0255.255.0.0
CIDR/17/18/19/20/21/22/23/24
Mask255.255.128.0255.255.192.0255.255.224.0255.255.240.0255.255.248.0255.255.252.0255.255.254.0255.255.255.0
CIDR/25/26/27/28/29/30/31/32
Mask255.255.255.128255.255.255.192255.255.255.224255.255.255.240255.255.255.248255.255.255.252255.255.255.254255.255.255.255

In practice, the exam (and real-world subnetting) almost always works within /8 through /32 — /1-/7 exist for completeness but you won't see them on questions.

Subnet mask cheat table (memorize this one)

This is the fastest way to answer subnetting questions — no full binary conversion needed once it's memorized.

Bits borrowed12345678
Mask octet128192224240248252254255
CIDR (of a /24)/25/26/27/28/29/30/31/32
Block size1286432168421

"Block size" = how far apart each subnet's network ID is. E.g. for a /27 (mask 224), subnets start at .0, .32, .64, .96... Usable hosts per subnet = block size − 2 (for the network ID and broadcast address).
